labF1.intro: This is a deterministic walkthrough of the data pipeline behind the race predictor, not a live model demo. Nothing here is a final accuracy, ROC-AUC, or best-model claim, that project is still in progress.

stages.title: Three data sources, wrapped for resilience
stages.body: Three sources feed the pipeline: Jolpica (historical results and qualifying), FastF1 (telemetry and lap data), and OpenF1 (live-timing-style session data), integrated across the 2022–2025 seasons. All three integrations wrap caching, retry with exponential backoff, and rate-limit handling, so a flaky API response degrades gracefully instead of failing the whole pipeline outright.

stages.title: From lap-level data to one race-entry table
stages.body: Roughly 100,000 lap-level records get processed into a 1,838-row race-entry master dataset, one row per driver per race. Combining the three sources this way first produced a many-to-many join explosion; fixed structurally with a bridge table, not a deduplication workaround.

stages.title: Data quality, treated as first-class work
stages.body: Before the dataset was trustworthy enough to build features on, it needed real data-quality work: weather coverage reconciliation, qualifying-time parsing, boolean-flag restoration, and DNF-label correction. I treat this as a first-class part of the project, not a footnote.

stages.title: Feature engineering without leaking the future
stages.body: Rolling-window features use shift(1), so a feature describing a driver's recent form only ever uses information from before the race it's predicting. Validation is time-based, not a random split, since a random split on time-series race data would silently let the model learn from future races when validating on past ones.

stages.title: Modelling: in progress, on purpose
stages.body: Target definition, model choice, and final validated results are still in progress. No accuracy, ROC-AUC, or best-model claim is published here yet; I'd rather leave it out than present something unstable as final. Progress is visible in the GitHub repository.

labSwiggy.intro: This is a deterministic walkthrough of the Swiggy Instamart assistant's agent graph, not a live integration. Every message, catalog item, and price on this page is scripted and mocked, on purpose: the real project has been tested end-to-end against a live Swiggy developer key, but the public site never makes that call. Pick a capability to see how a message routes through the graph.
labSwiggy.mockedNote: Every catalog item, price, and reply above is scripted and mocked. No real Swiggy account, catalog, or purchase is involved.
labSwiggy.brokeHeading: What broke, and what I learned

scenarios.label: Meal suggestions
scenarios.user: What can I make for dinner tonight?
scenarios.assistant: Based on your recent orders, you're probably low on onions and paneer. Here are 3 quick dinner ideas: paneer butter masala with rice, a simple dal and roti, or a vegetable pulao. Want me to price the missing ingredients for any of these?

steps.desc: Classifies the message as a meal-suggestion request
Infers what you probably have on hand from recent orders
Suggests meals and prices only the missing ingredients against the mocked catalog
Drafts the reply. No cart changes yet.

scenarios.label: Recurring grocery lists
scenarios.user: Create a list called Weekly Basics: milk and eggs, every Monday.
scenarios.assistant: Mocked demo: “Weekly Basics” (milk, large eggs) is scheduled for every Monday. When it's due, I'll surface it here for you to confirm or edit, I never order automatically.

steps.desc: Classifies the message as a recurring-list request
Matches “large eggs” to a real catalog item even though the wording doesn't match exactly
Registers a recurring job that checks whether the list is due
Confirms the schedule back to you

scenarios.label: Photo & voice discovery
scenarios.user: [uploads a photo of an empty ketchup bottle] (mocked)
scenarios.assistant: That looks like tomato ketchup. I found 3 matches in the mocked catalog. Want me to add the 500g bottle?

steps.desc: Classifies the message as a discovery request
Extracts a product description from the image or voice note
Searches the mocked catalog for matching products
Asks you to confirm the match before adding anything

scenarios.label: Recipe-to-cart planning
scenarios.user: I want to make biryani for 4 people.
scenarios.assistant: Mocked shopping list for biryani (serves 4): basmati rice, mixed vegetables, yogurt, biryani masala, and fried onions, checked against mocked live stock. One item, fried onions, is showing low stock, want a substitution, or should I add it anyway? Nothing goes into your cart until you approve.

steps.desc: Classifies the message as a recipe-planning request
Breaks the recipe into a scaled ingredient list
Checks each ingredient against the mocked catalog and proposes substitutions for anything low in stock
Waits for your explicit approval before touching the cart
Adds the approved items (mocked)

scenarios.label: Conversational cart editing
scenarios.user: Remove the onions, and make the tomatoes 2 instead of 1.
scenarios.assistant: Mocked demo: onions removed, tomato quantity changed from 1 to 2. Your cart is still just a draft, nothing is ordered yet.

steps.desc: Classifies the message as a cart-edit request
Parses the request into a structured, schema-validated cart operation
Applies the change to the mocked, server-side cart
Confirms exactly what changed

broke.title: Stale state
broke.body: Stale state carried over between conversation turns in ways mocked tests hadn't caught, once even triggering the cart-approval screen on an empty cart because a previous turn's pending items were never explicitly cleared. Fixing it became a regression test that later caught the identical bug in a different agent node.

broke.title: Router misclassification
broke.body: The intent router occasionally sent a message down the wrong capability path, like routing “I want [product]” to meal suggestions instead of cart editing. Fixed with an explicit routing rule rather than relying on the LLM classifier to generalize correctly on its own.

broke.title: Code-fenced JSON
broke.body: The LLM occasionally wrapped structured output in markdown code fences, breaking naive JSON parsing, even with an explicit instruction not to. Fixed with a shared parsing helper first, then moved cart operations to schema-validated structured output entirely.

broke.title: Dead node wiring
broke.body: One fully-built agent node had never actually run successfully: it was wired up with a decorator meant for a different function signature, so every call to it crashed silently until it was actually connected and exercised for the first time.

broke.title: Fallback search gaps
broke.body: A single failed catalog search, a synonym mismatch, or a quantity like “250g” in the query, used to just give up. Fixed with a bounded, deterministic fallback sequence, capped at a few attempts, no unbounded retrying, wired into every place the catalog gets searched.

broke.title: Address binding
broke.body: Instamart's cart is bound to a delivery address, which meant threading an address ID through every tool call that touches cart, search, or checkout, across every agent, not just one. A related gap surfaced later: the address selector was never actually wired into the UI, so every turn silently used whichever saved address came first.

broke.title: Mock-vs-live assumptions
broke.body: The fully mocked test suite passed cleanly, but testing against a real key surfaced bugs the mocks structurally couldn't catch, since the mocks were written under the same assumptions that caused those bugs. That's why both mocked tests and real-key testing matter: one proves the code does what it was told to, the other proves the assumptions about the outside world were right.
